sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>block layout of an equality Newton step</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">H   A^T</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">A   0</text></svg>
sections.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 block layout. The top-left block is labeled H, the top-right is labeled A transpose, the bottom-left is labeled A, and the bottom-right is labeled 0.
sections.body_md:
An unconstrained Newton step minimizes the quadratic model of \(f\). It solves \(H d=-\nabla f\), where \(H\) is the Hessian. On an equality \(Ax=b\) the step also has to keep the point feasible. At a point that already lies on the equality, the linearization says \(Ad=0\).

The multiplier \(\nu\) of the equality and the step \(d\) are unknowns of one linear system:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} H & A^T \\ A & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} d \\ \nu \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} -\nabla f \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The top block is stationarity of the quadratic model plus the constraint force \(A^T\nu\). The bottom block is \(Ad=0\). Adding \(d\) to a feasible point stays on \(Ax=b\).

If \(H\) is positive definite on the nullspace of \(A\), and \(A\) has full row rank, this matrix is nonsingular. Curvature in a direction that violates the equality is not required. A quadratic with that curvature finishes in one step.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For \(f=x^2+y^2\) the Hessian is \(2I\) and the gradient is \((2x,\ 2y)\). On \(x+y=s\) at a feasible start, the three equations are
\[
2\,dx+\nu=-\nabla_x f,\qquad 2\,dy+\nu=-\nabla_y f,\qquad dx+dy=0.
\]
The third equation forces the step along the line. The unconstrained system drops the third equation and the multiplier, and its landing point is feasible only by accident.

For \(\tfrac12 p x^2+\tfrac12 q y^2\) on \(x+y=b\), started at \((b,0)\), one step lands at \(x=bq/(p+q)\) and \(y=bp/(p+q)\). The coordinate with the smaller curvature takes more of the right-hand side.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(x^2+y^2\) subject to \(x+y=10\), starting at \((0,10)\). The gradient is \((0,\ 20)\). The system is \(2\,dx+
u=0\), \(2\,dy+
u=-20\), and \(dx+dy=0\). Then \(
u=-2\,dx\) and \(dy=-dx\), so \(-4\,dx=-20\) and \(dx=5\). The new point is \((5,\ 5)\), and the multiplier equals -10.

The point \((5,5)\) lies on the line and is the minimizer, because the objective is quadratic and the Hessian is positive definite. The unconstrained Newton step from the same start subtracts \((0,\ 10)\) and lands at the origin, where the coordinates sum to 0, not 10.

sections.heading: Pitfalls
sections.body_md:
Do not take the unconstrained step and then hope. At a feasible point the unconstrained step is feasible only when it already satisfies \(Ad=0\).

The right-hand side of the constraint block is zero only at a feasible point. If \(Ax\neq b\), that block is the residual \(b-Ax\), and the formula with a zero there does not apply.

A zero eigenvalue of \(H\) in an infeasible direction can be harmless. A zero eigenvalue in a feasible direction makes the block matrix singular, and the step is no longer defined as a unique solution. Negative curvature on the feasible subspace is a different failure: the quadratic model is then unbounded below on the equality.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md:
A log barrier changes the objective and keeps the equalities. The same block system is solved with the gradient and the Hessian of the barrier objective. The constraint matrix stays. The multiplier stays. Only the first block's derivatives change.

That is the Newton iteration inside a barrier method. The barrier weight, and the decision to send it toward zero, belong to the barrier skill. This skill is the linear system those iterations call.
